title: Pennsylvania Apprenticeships on the Move Grant 2026: Apply for Up to $249,999 to Expand Workforce Apprenticeship Programs
summary: The Commonwealth of Pennsylvania, through the Pennsylvania Department of Labor Industry (L I), has announced the Apprenticeships on the Move: Advancing Pennsylvania’s Workforce Grant , a major workforce development funding opportunity designed to strengthen apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship pathways across the state. Through this Notice of Grant Availability (NGA), approximately $4 million in state funding is available to eligible organizations seeking to develop new Registered Apprenticeship or Registered Pre-Apprenticeship programs or expand existing registered programs in Pennsylvania. Eligible applicants may request up to $249,999 to support projects that respond to employer workforce needs, build stronger talent pipelines, expand access to quality training, address barriers to employment, and create pathways into sustainable careers. The initiative is particularly focused on high-priority sectors including agriculture, energy, life sciences, manufacturing, robotics and technology, education, healthcare, and skilled trades. Applications for the Pennsylvania Apprenticeships on the Move Grant are due by October 2, 2026, at 4:00 PM Eastern Time . The anticipated grant performance period will run from May 1, 2027, through April 30, 2030 . Pennsylvania Apprenticeships on the Move Grant Overview The Apprenticeships on the Move initiative is intended to support Pennsylvania s long-term workforce and economic development objectives by increasing the number, accessibility, and effectiveness of Registered Apprenticeship and Registered Pre-Apprenticeship opportunities. The program recognizes that employers across Pennsylvania are facing increasing demand for skilled workers while also dealing with retirements, workforce shortages, competition for talent, and the loss of institutional knowledge. The grant therefore seeks to fund innovative approaches that connect employers, workforce organizations, education providers, labor organizations, community-based organizations, and other stakeholders to create sustainable workforce pipelines. Under the opportunity, organizations can propose either: Development of a new Registered Apprenticeship or Registered Pre-Apprenticeship program , or Expansion of an existing Registered Apprenticeship or Registered Pre-Apprenticeship program. Projects must operate within Pennsylvania and address workforce development needs in one or more of the eligible industry sectors identified by L I. How Much Funding Is Available? Approximately $4,000,000 has been allocated for the Apprenticeships on the Move initiative. Eligible applicants may request: Up to $249,999 per application Funding amounts aligned with the actual scope and needs of the proposed project Funding for eligible activities associated with developing or expanding apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship programs The exact amount awarded will depend on the funding requested, the quality and competitiveness of applications, available funds, and the evaluation conducted by L I. Pennsylvania may also provide additional funding during the grant period if funds become available through deobligation of other awards. Supplemental funding is not guaranteed and will depend on factors such as grantee performance, demonstrated need, ability to spend additional funds effectively, and continued alignment with the objectives of the grant. The grant is 100% state funded . What Is the Main Purpose of the Apprenticeships on the Move Grant? The central purpose of this grant is to strengthen Pennsylvania s workforce by supporting apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship programs that respond directly to employer and labor-market needs. The initiative seeks to: Develop new Registered Apprenticeship programs. Develop new Registered Pre-Apprenticeship programs. Expand existing registered apprenticeship programs. Expand existing registered pre-apprenticeship programs. Strengthen talent pipelines in high-demand industries. Increase access to apprenticeship opportunities. Help employers address workforce shortages. Provide individuals with skills and workplace experience. Support pathways to industry-recognized credentials. Address barriers preventing individuals from entering apprenticeship pathways. Increase participation among historically underserved and underrepresented populations. Encourage collaboration between employers, education providers, labor organizations, workforce boards, and community organizations. Strengthen Pennsylvania s long-term economic development priorities. Applicants are expected to demonstrate a clear connection between their proposed project and Pennsylvania s workforce and economic development priorities, including Governor Shapiro s Ten-Year Strategic Plan for Economic Development and the Pennsylvania Workforce Innovation and Opportunity Act (WIOA) Combined State Plan. Who Can Apply for the Grant? The opportunity is intended for organizations that can serve as sponsors or intermediaries for new or existing registered apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship programs in Pennsylvania. Eligible organizations may include: Businesses Community-based organizations Economic development organizations Industry associations Labor organizations Local education agencies Local workforce development boards Nonprofit organizations Postsecondary institutions Public libraries STEM ecosystems If an applicant is not the actual program sponsor, the application must provide significant evidence demonstrating that the program sponsor is an involved partner in the proposed project. The organization must also have the capacity to coordinate and manage the project, administer the financial aspects of the grant, collect and report performance information, and work with an evaluator. Two Types of Projects Can Be Funded 1. Development of a New Registered Apprenticeship or Pre-Apprenticeship Program Organizations may apply to establish a new apprenticeship or pre-apprenticeship program that has not yet been registered at the beginning of the grant performance period. The proposed program must ultimately be registered with the Commonwealth of Pennsylvania. Awardees will have up to one year from the contract start date to finalize registration or demonstrate progress toward registration. Grantees will be expected to establish and maintain communication with representatives of the Pennsylvania Apprenticeship and Training Office (ATO), which serves as the State Apprenticeship Agency (SAA), as they develop and register the program. Organizations that fail to make adequate progress toward registration may have funds deobligated. 2. Expansion of an Existing Registered Program Organizations may also apply to expand an existing Registered Apprenticeship or Registered Pre-Apprenticeship program that was already registered before the start of the grant performance period. For purposes of this grant, expansion means an increase in the number of participants enrolled in the program . Expansion does not include adding a new occupation to the existing program. Organizations seeking to expand an existing program must ensure that the program sponsor remains compliant with applicable federal and Pennsylvania laws, regulations, policies, standards, and approved program standards. Eligible Industry Sectors The proposed apprenticeship or pre-apprenticeship program must operate within at least one of the sectors identified by Pennsylvania L I. Eligible sectors are: Agriculture Projects may address workforce needs associated with agricultural occupations and the broader agricultural economy. Energy Programs may develop talent pipelines for energy-related occupations and emerging workforce requirements in the energy sector. Life Sciences Organizations working to develop skilled talent for life sciences industries may submit proposals within this sector. Manufacturing Manufacturing remains a major focus of Pennsylvania s workforce development strategy, and eligible projects may address skills shortages and talent pipeline needs within the sector. Robotics and Technology Programs focused on robotics, technology, and related occupations may qualify where they demonstrate clear workforce demand. Education Education-sector apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship initiatives may be eligible where they respond to identified workforce needs. Healthcare Healthcare workforce development projects may qualify under the healthcare sector. Skilled Trades The skilled trades category includes, but is not limited to: Construction Electrical work HVAC Steamfitting Fiber optics Telecommunications Applicants must identify the applicable sector or sectors in their application and demonstrate how the proposed project addresses workforce development needs within those sectors. Applications proposing programs outside the eligible sectors will be considered ineligible. What Is a Registered Apprenticeship? Registered Apprenticeship is a structured workforce development model that combines employment, training, mentorship, technical education, and recognized credentials. According to the grant announcement, Registered Apprenticeships have five key components: A paid job On-the-job training Related technical instruction Mentorship Credentials This combination allows participants to gain practical work experience while developing technical and occupational skills. For employers, apprenticeship programs can provide a structured way to develop and retain skilled workers. For participants, apprenticeships provide a pathway to earn wages while learning and working toward industry-recognized credentials. What Is a Registered Pre-Apprenticeship? Registered Pre-Apprenticeship programs are designed to prepare individuals for entry into Registered Apprenticeship programs. The grant identifies five core components of a registered pre-apprenticeship: An established connection to at least one existing Registered Apprenticeship program. Approved training and curriculum. Hands-on learning through appropriate program designs and approaches. An opportunity to earn an industry-recognized credential. Access to support services and career counseling. Pre-apprenticeship can therefore serve as an important bridge between education, workforce preparation, and formal apprenticeship. Why Is Pennsylvania Investing in Apprenticeships? Pennsylvania is experiencing workforce challenges driven by several factors. Employers are facing shortages of skilled workers, increased competition for talent, and the retirement of experienced workers. As experienced employees leave the workforce, organizations can lose decades of technical knowledge and operational expertise. Registered Apprenticeship programs can help address this challenge by combining experienced-worker mentorship with structured training for new employees. This allows organizations to facilitate knowledge transfer while preparing the next generation of workers. Apprenticeships also provide workers with opportunities to earn wages while acquiring skills and credentials, making them an important pathway into family-sustaining careers. Pennsylvania has historically used apprenticeship models in areas such as construction, manufacturing, and industrial occupations. The Commonwealth is now seeking to expand apprenticeship opportunities into sectors such as healthcare, education, agriculture, energy, life sciences, robotics, technology, and telecommunications. What Should Successful Projects Demonstrate? Applicants must clearly demonstrate that the proposed program responds to a real workforce need. A strong application should provide evidence such as: Labor market information Employer demand Workforce shortage data Talent pipeline gaps Economic development information Information about the occupations being targeted The number of apprentices or pre-apprentices expected to be served Information about the geographic area to be served Evidence of employer involvement Evidence of stakeholder partnerships The applicant must also explain how the project contributes to Pennsylvania s broader workforce and economic development goals. Priority Areas That Can Strengthen an Application The grant provides priority consideration for proposals demonstrating certain characteristics. Previously Unfunded Programs Priority may be given to new initiatives that have not previously received funding, including initiatives developed by existing Registered Apprenticeship or Pre-Apprenticeship sponsors. On-the-Job Learning, Related Technical Instruction and Supportive Services Priority consideration may be given to: Registered Apprenticeship programs using grant funds to support on-the-job learning, related technical instruction, and supportive services. Pre-Apprenticeship programs using grant funds to support paid work experience, related technical instruction, and supportive services. Applicants seeking this priority must reflect the relevant expenses in the applicable budget categories. Group Apprenticeship Models and Multi-County Programs Priority may be given to group Registered Apprenticeship models or pre-apprenticeship programs operating physically across multiple counties. For multi-county pre-apprenticeship replication, the program must have physical operations in at least three counties. Historically Underserved and Underrepresented Populations Applicants are encouraged to develop diverse talent pipelines that expand apprenticeship access for groups that have historically been underrepresented or underserved. These may include: Women People of color Individuals with disabilities Veterans Individuals from underserved or unserved communities Individuals who speak English as a second language Justice-impacted or adjudicated populations Individuals experiencing multiple barriers to employment Applicants should explain how their programs will identify and address barriers to education, training, and employment. Accessibility Priority consideration may also be given to projects that design, create, adjust, or upgrade physical and digital environments and services to improve accessibility for apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship participants. Labor Union Collaboration Applications demonstrating meaningful collaboration with labor unions can receive priority consideration. The labor union must either be the applicant or provide a letter of commitment explaining its specific role in the project. Potential involvement could include: Serving as an affiliated Registered Apprenticeship sponsor. Supporting curriculum development. Supporting a Registered Pre-Apprenticeship program. Providing continuing support after the grant period. Addressing Barriers to Apprenticeship Participation A major component of the opportunity is the expectation that projects address barriers that prevent people from entering or completing apprenticeship pathways. Applicants should consider barriers such as: Transportation challenges Basic skills deficiencies Socioeconomic limitations Program waitlists Program choice restrictions Workplace accessibility challenges Other barriers to education and employment Projects that provide meaningful solutions to these challenges can strengthen access to apprenticeship opportunities. Required Program Outcomes Applicants are expected to propose measurable participant and program outcomes. For new Registered Apprenticeship programs, the desired outcome is that 80% of participants either remain active apprentices or successfully complete the program . For group apprenticeship models, the same 80% target applies to participants. For Registered Pre-Apprenticeship programs, applicants must establish targets for completion and transition into the affiliated Registered Apprenticeship program. At least 30% of pre-apprentices who complete the program must matriculate into the affiliated Registered Apprenticeship program . The same 30% matriculation requirement applies to eligible pre-apprenticeship programs being replicated across multiple counties. Expansion projects are similarly expected to focus on participation, completion, retention, and progression into apprenticeship. Performance Metrics L I will work with successful applicants to establish performance metrics during the grant period. Applicants should propose measurable outputs and outcomes covering areas such as: Participant enrollment Participant demographics Continued participation Program completion Employer engagement Training provider engagement Apprentice and pre-apprentice participation Transition from pre-apprenticeship into apprenticeship Credentials obtained Participant wages Program impact Partnership activities Projects should also track the average wage of apprentices at the time of program completion. Grantees are expected to maintain secure, confidential, accurate, and complete participant records for verification and compliance purposes. Grant Evaluation Criteria Applications will be reviewed through an initial eligibility review followed by a merit-based evaluation. To be considered for funding, an application must achieve at least 70% of the total available score, equivalent to 84 out of 120 points . The evaluation structure is: Evaluation Area Points Project Design and Management Plan 25 Performance Outcomes 15 Impact and Sustainability 15 Stakeholder Engagement and Partnership 15 Other Selection Factors/Priority Considerations 35 Budget and Budget Justification 15 Total 120 This scoring structure makes it important for applicants to address every evaluation category directly and provide evidence rather than relying on general descriptions. Project Design and Management Plan This section is worth 25 points . Applicants should clearly explain: The workforce need being addressed. The population to be served. Employers involved. Occupations targeted. Geographic area covered. Relevant labor market information. Employer demand. Workforce shortages. Talent pipeline gaps. The number of apprentices or pre-apprentices to be served. How traditionally underserved populations will be reached. How the project aligns with Pennsylvania s WIOA Combined State Plan. How the project aligns with Pennsylvania s economic development priorities. The implementation timeline. Cohort start and completion dates. Key milestones. Registration steps. Long-term sustainability. Potential for scaling and replication. Applicants must use the required timeline template in Appendix D. Performance Outcomes This category is worth 15 points . Applicants must describe their intended outcomes and explain how those outcomes will be measured. The application should include: Goals Services Expected outcomes Number of people to be served Performance indicators Enrollment targets Completion targets Employer engagement Training provider engagement Participant retention Wage outcomes The Goals and Outcomes Table in Appendix E must be used as required. Impact and Sustainability This category is worth 15 points . Applicants should explain how the project will contribute to the broader goals of the Apprenticeships on the Move initiative. They should identify: Credentials participants will receive. Expected impact on participants. Expected impact on employers. Impact of partnerships. Data tracking and reporting capacity. Recruitment metrics. Participation metrics. Completion and accomplishment metrics. Long-term sustainability. Applicants must also complete the Sustainability Plan in Appendix F. The sustainability strategy should explain how the apprenticeship or pre-apprenticeship program will continue after the grant period ends. Stakeholder Engagement and Partnerships This section is worth 15 points . Applicants should identify the organizations and stakeholders involved in the proposed project and clearly define their roles. Potential partners may include: Employers Workforce development organizations Educational institutions Community-based organizations Labor organizations Economic development organizations Workforce boards Training providers Applications should explain the responsibilities of each partner and demonstrate that the applicant has the capacity to coordinate the partnership effectively. Key personnel should also be identified by name, along with their roles and contributions to the project. Sector Diversity Pennsylvania is also seeking diversity among funded sectors. No more than three awards may be made to applications supporting the same industry sector , even where projects serve different geographic areas. Applicants should therefore clearly identify the sector or sectors their project supports and explain how their proposal responds to workforce needs in that sector. Budget Requirements The proposed budget must be directly connected to the project narrative. Applicants should provide: Detailed budget line items. Requested funds. Leveraged funds. Costs by category. Quantities. Unit costs where applicable. Detailed justification for expenditures. Explanation of how expenditures support project activities and deliverables. Costs that are not discussed in the proposal should not appear in the budget. Administrative costs may not exceed 10% of the total amount requested . The budget must cover the entire performance period from May 1, 2027, to April 30, 2030 . Reimbursement-Based Funding Applicants should understand that this grant does not operate as an upfront lump-sum payment. Grant expenses are reimbursed after they have been incurred and documented. Monthly invoices must be supported by appropriate documentation. Organizations should therefore have sufficient financial and administrative capacity to manage expenses, maintain records, and submit invoices properly. Awardees must document expenses consistently with Generally Accepted Accounting Principles. Supporting documentation may include evidence such as: Invoices Competitive bidding documentation Time records Payroll documentation Other appropriate expenditure records Employee time charged to the grant must accurately reflect the actual amount of time spent working on grant activities. Important Restriction for New Programs Organizations developing new Registered Apprenticeship or Pre-Apprenticeship programs should pay particular attention to the registration requirement. New programs cannot invoice for: On-the-Job Training (OJT) Related Technical Instruction (RTI) Supportive services before the new apprenticeship or pre-apprenticeship program has been approved. These expenses must be incurred after program approval. Pennsylvania SAP Vendor Identification Number Applicants are required to have a Pennsylvania SAP Vendor Identification Number . The number can be obtained at no cost through the applicable Pennsylvania vendor registration process. Applicants should begin this process early because obtaining the vendor number may take up to two weeks. An organization may submit its application before receiving the number if necessary, but a grant will not be awarded without documentation of the required Pennsylvania Vendor Identification Number. Applicants unable to meet this requirement at the time of award may have to relinquish the award. Fiscal Agent Requirements A fiscal agent is an organization that accepts responsibility for managing grant funds on behalf of the grantee. The fiscal agent may be a business, school, workforce organization, or another eligible organization capable of managing the financial requirements of the award. The fiscal agent is responsible for areas such as: Fiscal accounting Invoicing Payments State and federal tax reporting Financial documentation Audit requirements A fiscal agent must also obtain employee dishonesty/theft insurance of at least $100,000 . Organizations that can manage the fiscal responsibilities themselves may serve as their own fiscal agents. Where Local Workforce Development Boards apply as a region, the region must designate a single LWDB as the lead applicant and fiscal agent. Application Package Requirements Applicants must download and complete the official application documents provided by Pennsylvania L I. The application package must include several components. 1. Application Form The Application Form must: Be completed in full. Be no more than one page. Be saved as a single file. Follow the required naming convention: ApplicantName_App_Form . 2. Project Summary Cover The Project Summary Cover must not exceed three pages. It should include: Applicant name Fiscal agent name Vendor ID number Unique Entity Identifier, where applicable Project title Project county Project service area Municipality House and Senate districts served Project partners Brief project summary Project point of contact Contact information 3. Project Narrative The Project Narrative is a central part of the application and may be up to 10 pages , excluding the Goals/Outcomes Table, Timeline, and Sustainability Plan attachments. How to Submit the Application Completed application packages must be submitted electronically by email to the Pennsylvania Apprenticeship and Training Office Grants resource account: ATOGrants@pa.gov The application must be submitted no later than: October 2, 2026, at 4:00 PM ET Late applications will not be accepted. Important Grant Timeline Applicants should take note of the following dates: August 12, 2026: Notice of Grant Availability released. August 26, 2026 at 9:00 AM ET: Bidder s Conference. September 8, 2026 at 4:00 PM ET: Deadline for submitting questions. October 2, 2026 at 4:00 PM ET: Application deadline. May 1, 2027: Anticipated performance period start. April 30, 2030: Anticipated contract end date. Grant Award and Notification Process Funding will be awarded competitively based on the availability of funds and the quality of submitted applications. L I expects to notify applicants by email within 30 days following the award determination . Applicants whose proposals are not selected may request a feedback call within 30 days of receiving their denial notification. Successful applicants will be required to enter into a Workforce Grant Agreement with L I unless they already have an applicable grant agreement in place. Reporting and Monitoring Requirements Successful grantees will have substantial reporting responsibilities. A strong proposal should: Clearly identify a genuine workforce problem. Support the problem statement with labor-market and employer-demand evidence. Identify the specific occupations and sector being targeted. Clearly define the population and geographic area to be served. Demonstrate meaningful employer participation. Build strong cross-sector partnerships. Explain how the project will increase apprenticeship participation. Address barriers to entry and completion. Establish measurable participant targets. Provide realistic completion and retention goals. Demonstrate a clear pathway from pre-apprenticeship into Registered Apprenticeship where applicable. Explain how participants will obtain credentials. Provide a detailed implementation timeline. Demonstrate a credible path toward program registration where a new program is proposed. Related technical instruction. On-the-job learning. Mentorship. Credentials. Program partners. Registration milestones. Engagement with the Apprenticeship and Training Office. The objective is to establish apprenticeship and pre-apprenticeship systems that remain useful to employers and workers after grant funding has ended. Instead of treating workforce training as a standalone activity, the initiative encourages collaboration among businesses, educational institutions, workforce boards, community organizations, labor organizations, and other stakeholders. title: Charles Darwin University RTP Scholarship 2026/27: Research Funding for PhD and Master by Research Students in Australia
summary: Charles Darwin University (CDU) offers Australian Government Research Training Program (RTP) Scholarships to high-performing Higher Degree by Research candidates undertaking a Doctor of Philosophy (PhD) or Master by Research in Australia. The RTP is one of Australia’s principal funding mechanisms for postgraduate research. At Charles Darwin University, scholarships are awarded competitively to candidates who demonstrate strong academic performance, substantial research preparation, high-quality research outputs or research experience, and alignment with CDU’s research priorities. Both domestic and international candidates can meet the general RTP eligibility framework, although the availability of scholarships differs substantially between the two groups and between specific research projects. For 2026, CDU lists an RTP stipend of: AUD $35,489 per year for full-time students, tax-free and paid fortnightly. For part-time recipients, the published 2026 rate is: AUD $17,744.50 per year, taxable and paid fortnightly. CDU states that stipend support normally runs for three years for a doctoral degree and two years for a research Master’s degree . Additional benefits can include paid sick leave, maternity leave and a relocation allowance of up to AUD $2,000 for domestic recipients and AUD $2,500 for international recipients , subject to conditions. However, prospective applicants should pay close attention to an important update before relying on social-media posts advertising a general “2027 RTP Scholarship” with a 30 September 2026 deadline . Important Application Status Update The current official CDU information does not support advertising the RTP as a general open application round with a confirmed 30 September 2026 closing date. CDU’s current RTP information page states that: Research Training Program Scholarships are by invitation only. Applicants must first be invited by the CDU Higher Degree by Research team before they can submit the formal RTP scholarship application. In addition, CDU’s current project-focused scholarship information indicates that scholarship opportunities for 2026/27 are attached to pre-approved research projects and primarily target new HDR candidates . The university’s most recent international scholarship information says the International PhD RTP Scholarship is closed and that no international RTP scholarships remain for Semester 1, 2027, while future opportunities may be announced later. Therefore, the frequently circulated statement that the “Charles Darwin University RTP Scholarship 2027 is open to all nationalities until 30 September 2026” should not currently be presented as an official CDU deadline . Applicants should instead follow the live CDU scholarship pages and, where applicable, the instructions associated with a specific research project. Official CDU RTP information About the Australian Government Research Training Program The Research Training Program is funded by the Australian Government and administered through eligible Australian universities. Rather than students applying directly to the Australian Government, the government provides funding to participating higher education providers, and each university manages its own: Scholarship application system Eligibility process Ranking process Selection process Scholarship conditions The Australian Government confirms that RTP funding supports both domestic and overseas students undertaking research doctorates and research Master’s degrees at eligible Australian higher education institutions. RTP support can take three broad forms: Tuition fee offsets Stipends for general living expenses Allowances associated with the additional costs of undertaking higher-degree research At Charles Darwin University, which forms of support a candidate receives can depend on their scholarship type, citizenship status and the particular research opportunity. What Degrees Are Eligible at Charles Darwin University? For RTP purposes, CDU defines Higher Degree by Research programmes as: Doctor of Philosophy and: Master by Research The scholarship is therefore not intended for ordinary coursework degrees such as: Taught Master’s programmes Graduate certificates Graduate diplomas Undergraduate programmes CDU’s current eligibility guidelines explicitly state that the relevant HDR programmes are the Doctor of Philosophy and Master by Research . Charles Darwin University PhD Opportunities CDU is currently promoting a project-focused scholarship model for 2026/27. The university lists pre-approved HDR projects across strategic research fields and allows new applicants to submit expressions of interest directly to relevant project supervisors. Research areas represented across CDU projects include subjects such as: Indigenous studies Ecology Remote health Energy Artificial intelligence Sustainability Specific eligibility and scholarship availability can differ by project, so candidates should not assume that every PhD project automatically includes the same funding package. Current Domestic Scholarship Opportunities For domestic candidates, CDU currently lists opportunities including the: RTP Domestic PhD Scholarship which provides approximately the standard CDU RTP stipend together with an RTP fee offset covering PhD tuition fees for up to three years. CDU also lists a: DVCRCC Domestic Strategic Project Scholarship which may combine the standard RTP stipend with an additional top-up of up to approximately AUD $18,000 per year , together with a full fee offset for up to three years. These project-specific opportunities demonstrate why applicants should review the actual project listing rather than assuming that every CDU research scholarship has identical financial conditions. Current International Scholarship Position International candidates need to exercise particular caution. The general RTP framework does permit international applicants, and CDU’s eligibility rules explicitly state that both domestic and international students can be eligible for consideration. However, that does not mean that unrestricted international RTP places are always available. CDU’s current project-focused scholarship page states that the International PhD RTP Scholarship for international applicants is highly limited, while the most recent scholarship listing indicates that it is closed and not accepting applications , with no international RTP scholarships currently left for Semester 1, 2027. CDU does separately advertise Graduate Full Fee Scholarships for selected international HDR applicants, covering tuition fees for eligible research programmes. International applicants should therefore distinguish carefully between: RTP stipend funding Tuition-only scholarships Project-specific scholarships Other international research scholarships A tuition waiver alone is not the same as receiving an RTP living stipend. How Much Is the CDU RTP Stipend? CDU currently publishes the 2026 stipend rate as: Full-Time Students AUD $35,489 per year The stipend is: Tax-free Paid in fortnightly instalments Part-Time Students AUD $17,744.50 per year The part-time stipend is: Taxable Paid fortnightly These are CDU’s stated 2026 rates. Applicants should not automatically describe AUD $35,489 as the confirmed 2027 CDU stipend unless CDU publishes that figure for 2027. The Australian Government separately establishes indexed RTP base and maximum stipend rates nationally each year. For 2027, the federal minimum full-time RTP stipend rate is listed as AUD $35,550 , but universities can set their institutional scholarship rate within the permitted range. CDU applicants should therefore use the university’s own rate once its 2027 amount is formally published. How Long Does RTP Funding Last? CDU’s current scholarship information states that stipend funding normally runs for: Three years full-time for a doctoral degree and: Two years for a research Master’s degree. The broader Australian Government framework allows universities some flexibility over doctoral RTP support periods, but university-specific scholarship conditions ultimately determine the individual recipient’s funded period. Candidates should therefore read the CDU scholarship offer and conditions carefully if selected. Tuition Fee Support Tuition arrangements differ between domestic and international research candidates. Domestic RTP Fee Offset Domestic RTP recipients can receive a: Full RTP fee offset which covers eligible research degree tuition costs for the standard funded period. For project-based domestic PhD scholarships, CDU states that the fee offset can cover PhD tuition fees for up to three years. International Tuition Fee Support For international candidates, tuition support is more limited and competitive. CDU indicates that international applicants awarded an RTP stipend may receive a Graduate Full Fee Scholarship covering international Higher Degree by Research tuition fees for the normal degree period. CDU’s course information explains that these international tuition fee waivers are limited and normally cover: Three years full-time for a PhD Two years full-time for a Master by Research International candidates who do not receive a fee-waiver scholarship may instead receive an offer as a full fee-paying research student. For this reason, describing the CDU RTP as automatically covering tuition for every international candidate would be inaccurate. Relocation Allowance CDU also identifies relocation support as one of the possible RTP benefits. The current published maximum allowance is: Up to AUD $2,000 for domestic students and: Up to AUD $2,500 for international students subject to applicable conditions. Candidates should review the scholarship terms to determine: Eligible relocation expenses Documentation required Claim deadlines Whether reimbursement or another payment method applies Paid Leave Benefits Additional benefits listed by CDU include: Paid sick leave Maternity leave The precise conditions and entitlements depend on the scholarship rules. Candidates with family, medical or caregiving considerations should consult CDU’s RTP conditions rather than assuming ordinary employment leave rules apply. Who Can Be Considered for the CDU RTP Scholarship? The current CDU RTP eligibility framework requires candidates to satisfy five broad conditions. Applicants must: Be a domestic or international candidate. Meet CDU academic and English-language admission requirements. Be invited to apply by the CDU HDR team. Submit a complete RTP scholarship application by the deadline communicated to them. Not receive equivalent financial support from another source for their HDR studies. The third requirement is particularly important: The formal RTP application is invitation-only. A prospective student therefore cannot necessarily submit an unrestricted scholarship application simply because they meet the academic criteria. What Counts as a Domestic Student? CDU defines domestic students as: Australian citizens Australian permanent residents New Zealand citizens Other applicants are generally categorized as international students. Academic Requirements for a Master by Research For scholarship ranking, Master by Research applicants are expected to demonstrate relevant research training. CDU states that applicants should have completed at least: Half a semester full-time equivalent or: 20 credit points of research activity at AQF Level 8 or above within a relevant qualification. The university assesses both: Academic performance Quality and amount of previous research preparation Academic Requirements for PhD Applicants PhD applicants need stronger prior research preparation. CDU states that candidates should have completed at least: One semester full-time equivalent or: 40 credit points of research activity at AQF Level 8 or above. Relevant evidence can include: Research thesis Dissertation Research units Honours research Master’s research components Applicants must clearly identify which parts of previous degrees involved research and how heavily those units were weighted. General HDR Entry Standard For project-focused PhD opportunities, CDU summarizes its HDR academic expectation as a Bachelor’s or Master’s degree with a: Distinction-level GPA together with appropriate research preparation. If a candidate does not meet the research-unit requirement exactly, CDU may consider equivalent research experience where the applicant can demonstrate a sufficiently strong research record. This flexibility is especially relevant to candidates whose home universities use different programme structures. International English-Language Requirements International applicants must also satisfy CDU’s English requirements. For the current project scholarship campaign, CDU provides an example of: IELTS 6.5 overall, with no individual band below 6.0 and also notes acceptance of the: Duolingo English Test and other approved tests. Applicants should check the requirements for their specific HDR programme because accepted tests and exemptions can vary. Scholarship Selection Is Highly Competitive Meeting the minimum admission conditions does not mean that an applicant will receive an RTP scholarship. CDU states clearly that: Australian Government RTP Stipend Scholarships are awarded to students of exceptional research potential and are not automatically granted to all HDR students. Scholarship applications are ranked competitively. CDU currently evaluates applicants across four broad areas: Qualifications and academic performance Quality research publications and non-traditional research outputs Research experience or portfolio Alignment with strategic research priorities Academic Performance Academic results form an important part of the ranking process. CDU expects applicants to demonstrate: Strong GPA Relevant Bachelor’s, Honours or Master’s qualifications Adequate research training Strong thesis or dissertation performance International applicants must make their grading systems understandable to CDU. This may require submitting: Official transcripts Grading scale explanations Course or unit outlines Thesis information Official English translations Research Publications Research outputs can significantly strengthen an RTP application. CDU says successful candidates will typically demonstrate recent, high-quality: Peer-reviewed research publications as either: First author Co-author The university can also consider eligible: Non-Traditional Research Outputs such as creative or discipline-specific research products where appropriate. Candidates may submit up to four primary outputs demonstrating their research quality, impact and relevance. Quality Matters More Than Quantity CDU explicitly advises candidates to focus on: Quality over quantity. Listing a large number of publications without evidence of their quality will not necessarily make an application stronger. Applicants should therefore identify their strongest work and provide evidence such as: DOI Journal ranking Peer-review status Publisher information Publication details Research impact Publications Must Be Formally Accepted CDU does not treat all unpublished manuscripts equally. Outputs must generally be: Published In press Formally accepted after peer review Manuscripts that are merely: Submitted Under review In revision are not assessed as completed research outputs for scholarship ranking. This distinction is especially important for early-career researchers preparing an application close to the scholarship assessment period. Research Experience Applicants may also receive credit for broader research experience not already captured by academic qualifications or publications. Relevant experience can include: Research employment Work at a reputable university Research institute employment Research-related professional work Other recognised research outputs Substantial research portfolio CDU requires claims to be supported with clear documentation. Strategic Research Alignment CDU may give additional weight to research proposals that align with: University strategic research priorities Institutional research strengths Existing research capabilities This makes supervisor and project fit especially important. An academically excellent applicant proposing work unrelated to available expertise may be less competitive than a candidate whose research fits strongly within an established CDU team. What Does a Strong Applicant Look Like? CDU’s current project scholarship guidance says strong applicants will generally have a combination of: Excellent academic record Honours or Master’s research training High GPA Research publications Practical research experience Skills aligned with the project The university notes that highly competitive applicants typically have at least one strong publication, such as a quality journal article, or a Master by Research/MPhil with a GPA of around 80% or higher . This is indicative of competitiveness rather than a universal minimum requirement for every project. How the Current Application Process Works The current CDU process is not simply: “Fill out an RTP scholarship form before September 30.” For project-focused opportunities, applicants generally begin with an: Expression of Interest to the lead supervisor. The EOI should include: A cover email explaining PhD eligibility, suitability for the research project and motivation Curriculum vitae Relevant qualifications and research experience Up to four strong publications where possible Postgraduate transcripts Grading system information Evidence of thesis or research components Key Details at a Glance University: Charles Darwin University Country: Australia Funding programme: Australian Government Research Training Program Study level: Higher Degree by Research Eligible degrees: Doctor of Philosophy and Master by Research CDU full-time stipend: AUD $35,489 per year at the published 2026 rate Part-time stipend: AUD $17,744.50 per year at the published 2026 rate Payment: Fortnightly Full-time stipend tax status: Tax-free Doctoral stipend duration: Normally three years at CDU Master by Research duration: Normally two years Relocation allowance: Up to AUD $2,000 domestic / AUD $2,500 international, subject to conditions Other benefits: Paid sick leave and maternity leave Domestic eligibility: Australian citizens, Australian permanent residents and New Zealand citizens International eligibility: International applicants can meet general RTP eligibility, subject to scholarship availability Formal scholarship application: By invitation only Current international 2027 status: International RTP availability is extremely limited; CDU’s latest public information indicates no general international Semester 1, 2027 RTP places remain Tips for Prospective Applicants 1. Find a Suitable Research Project First CDU’s current scholarship model strongly emphasizes pre-approved projects. Start by identifying: Research topic Faculty Supervisor Project fit before worrying about the formal RTP application. 2. Contact the Lead Supervisor A strong initial email should explain: Your research background Why you meet CDU PhD or Master by Research admission requirements Why you fit the project Your strongest research achievements Why you want to work with that supervisor Avoid generic mass emails. 3. Make Your Research Training Easy to Assess International degree structures can differ significantly from Australia’s. Clearly show: Which courses were research-based Credit weighting Thesis length Thesis grade Research methodology training CDU states that it is the applicant’s responsibility to make this information clear. 4. Provide Your Strongest Research Outputs If you have publications, prioritize the strongest four. Explain: Journal quality Peer review DOI Your contribution Relevance to the proposed research 5. Do Not Assume Admission Equals Scholarship An applicant may be academically eligible for a PhD but not competitive enough for RTP funding. Scholarship selection is substantially more competitive than minimum programme admission. 6. International Applicants Should Check Availability Before Spending Time on a Full Application This is especially important for 2027. CDU’s current information indicates very limited or closed international RTP availability for Semester 1, 2027. Contact the relevant supervisor or CDU HDR team before preparing a large application package. Conclusion The Charles Darwin University Research Training Program Scholarship remains an attractive Australian postgraduate research funding pathway for highly competitive candidates pursuing a PhD or Master by Research . CDU’s published 2026 full-time RTP stipend is AUD $35,489 per year , paid fortnightly and tax-free. Part-time recipients receive AUD $17,744.50 annually, taxable. Scholarship benefits can also include tuition support, paid leave and relocation assistance. The scholarship is competitive rather than automatic. Applicants are ranked according to factors including academic performance, research preparation, publications, broader research experience and alignment with CDU research priorities. Importantly, CDU’s current system requires candidates to be invited by the HDR team before submitting a formal RTP application . Please visit RTP Scholarship Ranking Guidelines before applying. title: UC Berkeley–Packard Foundation Philanthropy Fellow 2026: Apply for a $90,000 Professional Opportunity in Civil Society and Leadership

The Philanthropy Fellow position is situated within this broader environment of learning, leadership, innovation, and public impact. Haas is known for a culture that encourages innovation, collaboration, leadership, and continuous learning. The initiative operates under the Foundation s Just Societies goal while supporting work connected to the Foundation s other major goals and geographic areas of operation. At least two years of experience working in a full-time professional position. A bachelor s degree in a related area or equivalent experience and training. Experience working in civil society organizations. title: 2027 Tools Competition: Multi-Million-Dollar Funding Opportunity for Innovative Education Technology, AI Tools and Learning Datasets
summary: The 2027 Tools Competition is now open, inviting innovators, education technology developers, researchers, entrepreneurs, organisations and other solution-builders to propose tools and public infrastructure that can improve learning, teaching and access to opportunity. The competition supports education technology innovation that uses digital technology, data, artificial intelligence and learning science to address urgent challenges facing learners and educators. Its seventh cycle comes at a time when artificial intelligence is becoming increasingly common in education, work and everyday life, creating new opportunities while also raising important questions about trust, safety, privacy, effectiveness and responsible implementation. Rather than rewarding technology simply because it is new, the 2027 Tools Competition seeks proposals that demonstrate how tools can produce meaningful results in real-world learning environments. Strong proposals should explain how their solutions can be responsibly used, trusted, sustained and adapted to the needs of learners, educators and institutions. The Tools Competition is a programme of Renaissance Philanthropy and is organised by The Learning Agency . About the 2027 Tools Competition The Tools Competition is a multi-million-dollar funding opportunity focused on education technology innovation. It supports tools and public infrastructure that use digital technology, big data and learning science to respond to pressing needs across education and workforce development. The 2027 competition recognises that technology access alone does not automatically improve learning outcomes. A tool must be relevant to the learning context, easy to use, inclusive, evidence-informed and designed with the realities of learners and educators in mind. The competition therefore encourages proposals that address questions such as: Does the tool help learners understand what they know and what they still need to learn? Does it provide timely and useful support? Does it strengthen teaching practice rather than create unnecessary burdens? Does it make learning more engaging, practical and learner-driven? Does it help individuals navigate education-to-work transitions? Does it improve the availability of high-quality education data? Does it protect privacy, promote safety and support responsible technology use? Can the solution be sustained and used effectively in real learning environments? The strongest proposals will be those that demonstrate not only what technology or artificial intelligence can do, but also how the proposed solution can be implemented responsibly and generate meaningful benefits. Why the Competition Matters Artificial intelligence and digital tools are rapidly changing how people learn, work and access information. Many learners are already using generative AI to complete assignments, improve efficiency, understand difficult concepts and support their learning. However, the increasing use of AI in education also creates challenges. Learners may not always know whether information generated by AI is accurate. Educators may lack guidance on how to integrate AI into instruction. Institutions may face concerns about privacy, unequal access, bias, academic integrity and the long-term effects of technology on learning. The 2027 Tools Competition responds to this changing environment by encouraging the development of tools that are grounded in evidence and designed around actual learning needs. The competition places particular emphasis on solutions that: Improve the quality and usefulness of learning experiences. Support educators in delivering effective instruction. Provide inclusive and actionable information about student progress. Help learners become more independent and confident. Connect education with real-world opportunities. Strengthen the infrastructure needed for future education research and development. Integrate safety, privacy and responsibility into design and implementation. This approach moves beyond technology for its own sake. It focuses on whether a tool can make education more effective, equitable, engaging and responsive. 2027 Tools Competition Tracks The 2027 Tools Competition features four main tracks. These tracks cover K–12 education, postsecondary learning, the transition from education to work, and the development of high-quality datasets. Applicants should review the tracks carefully and select the one that most closely matches the purpose, users and intended impact of their tool or idea. 1. Strengthening Teaching The Strengthening Teaching track focuses on tools that improve instructional effectiveness while also making the teaching profession more sustainable. Teachers often face multiple demands, including lesson planning, assessment, classroom management, administrative responsibilities, reporting and adapting instruction to different learner needs. Technology can help reduce unnecessary workload and provide educators with better information for making instructional decisions. This track seeks tools that can support teachers in meaningful and practical ways. Proposed solutions should demonstrate how they can improve teaching quality, support professional practice and contribute to a more sustainable teaching environment. Potential areas of focus may include: Tools that support lesson planning and instructional preparation. Systems that help educators identify student learning needs. Platforms that provide timely instructional feedback. Resources that improve classroom engagement. Tools that reduce repetitive administrative work. Solutions that support differentiated instruction. Technologies that help teachers access and use evidence. Tools that strengthen collaboration and professional learning. A strong proposal for this track should explain how the tool supports educators without replacing professional judgement or adding unnecessary complexity. Applicants can learn more through the official Strengthening Teaching track page: Explore the Strengthening Teaching track 2. Reimagining Assessment The Reimagining Assessment track focuses on tools that strengthen K–12 assessment by providing more continuous, actionable and inclusive information about student learning. Traditional assessments may provide only a limited picture of what students know at a particular point in time. The competition encourages solutions that help educators and learners understand progress more continuously and use assessment information to improve learning. Tools under this track may support the collection, interpretation and use of learning evidence in ways that are timely and useful. Potential areas of focus may include: Formative assessment tools. Systems that identify learning gaps. Platforms that provide immediate feedback. Inclusive assessment approaches for diverse learners. Tools that help teachers adjust instruction. Solutions that make assessment more meaningful and less burdensome. Technologies that provide clearer information about student progress. Assessment tools that support personalised learning pathways. Successful proposals should explain how the tool can produce reliable information and how that information can be used to improve learning outcomes. Applicants can learn more through the official Reimagining Assessment track page: Explore the Reimagining Assessment track 3. Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work The Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work track focuses on tools that help learners build the skills, relationships, information and support needed to navigate education and employment in an increasingly AI-driven world. The transition from secondary education to higher education, vocational training or employment can be difficult. Learners may need help identifying suitable programmes, developing relevant skills, finding mentors, understanding career pathways, building professional networks and making informed decisions. This track seeks solutions that support learners during these transition points and help them connect education with real-world opportunities. Potential areas of focus may include: Career exploration and guidance tools. Platforms connecting learners with mentors or professionals. Tools that help students identify skills gaps. Systems supporting postsecondary planning. Resources that connect learners to internships, apprenticeships or jobs. Tools that help learners build professional networks. Technologies that support career readiness. Platforms that improve access to information about education and work opportunities. Solutions that help learners make informed decisions in changing labour markets. Proposals should demonstrate how the tool can help learners navigate uncertainty with greater clarity, confidence and connection. Applicants can learn more through the official Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work track page: Explore the Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work track 4. Building Better Datasets The Building Better Datasets track focuses on high-quality education datasets that can support future research, product development and innovation. Data is essential for understanding learning, evaluating educational tools and developing systems that respond to the needs of diverse learners. However, education datasets may be incomplete, difficult to access, poorly documented or insufficiently representative of different populations and learning environments. This track encourages the development of datasets that capture the diversity of learners, educational contexts and learning settings. High-quality datasets may help researchers and developers: Study learning patterns and outcomes. Improve education technology tools. Develop and evaluate artificial intelligence systems. Understand differences across learning environments. Support evidence-based education policy. Improve the inclusiveness and reliability of educational research. Identify gaps in existing education data. Develop tools that are more responsive to real-world needs. Applicants should explain the value of the proposed dataset, the population or learning context it represents, how the data will be collected or developed, and how privacy, consent, security and responsible use will be addressed. Applicants can learn more through the official Building Better Datasets track page: Explore the Building Better Datasets track What Types of Proposals Are Encouraged? The competition is intended for proposals that address important challenges in learning, teaching and opportunity. While the specific requirements may differ by track, strong proposals are likely to demonstrate several important qualities. Evidence-informed design Proposals should be grounded in relevant research, learning science, user experience evidence or practical knowledge of the problem being addressed. Applicants should explain why the proposed solution is likely to work and what evidence supports its approach. Clear understanding of the target users Applicants should identify who will use or benefit from the tool. Depending on the track, target users may include: K–12 students. Teachers and school leaders. Postsecondary students. Adult learners. Career seekers. Researchers. Education institutions. Workforce development organisations. Policymakers. Developers and education technology providers. A strong proposal should demonstrate an understanding of the needs, constraints and experiences of the intended users. Real-world usefulness The competition is focused on tools that can function in real learning environments. Applicants should explain how their proposed solution will be used in practice and what problem it will solve. Proposals should avoid focusing only on technical novelty. They should demonstrate how the tool will create practical value for learners, educators, institutions or researchers. Responsible technology use Safety, privacy and responsibility are central to the 2027 competition. Applicants should consider how their tool will protect users and avoid potential harm. Relevant considerations may include: Data privacy. Informed consent. Data security. Bias and fairness. Accessibility. Transparency. Responsible artificial intelligence. Protection of children and vulnerable users. Appropriate human oversight. Accountability in design and implementation. Potential for sustainability and scale Strong proposals should consider how the tool can be maintained, adopted and sustained beyond an initial pilot. Applicants may need to explain the resources, partnerships, infrastructure or implementation strategies required for long-term use. Who Should Consider Applying? The competition may be relevant to a broad range of individuals and organisations working on education technology, learning science, digital infrastructure and workforce development. Potential applicants may include: Education technology startups. Non-profit organisations. Researchers and research teams. Universities and academic institutions. Education-focused companies. Developers and technology innovators. Social enterprises. Data scientists. Learning designers. Educators developing innovative tools. Organisations working in K–12 education. Organisations supporting postsecondary learners. Workforce development organisations. Teams developing education datasets. Collaborations involving researchers, educators, technologists and community organisations. Applicants should consult the official competition rules and the specific requirements for their preferred track before preparing a submission. The overview page alone does not provide a complete list of all eligibility conditions, submission requirements, funding amounts per award or selection criteria. Geographic Eligibility The 2027 Tools Competition overview describes its goal as supporting learning, teaching and opportunity needs in real-world settings and refers to learners worldwide. However, the provided overview does not explicitly state a complete country-by-country eligibility list or a definitive nationality restriction. Therefore, individuals and organisations from outside the United States should review the official eligibility requirements, rules and submission information to confirm whether they can apply. Applicants from Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, South America, the Caribbean, Oceania and other regions should not assume eligibility solely based on the global focus of the competition. The official eligibility quiz and rules should be consulted for clarification: Check eligibility through the official eligibility quiz Read the official competition rules Application and Submission Information The competition’s official website provides a Submit Here link for applicants who are ready to submit their proposals. Applicants should review the relevant track page and official rules before submitting. They should ensure that their proposal addresses the specific problem, target users, expected impact and implementation context associated with the selected track. A strong submission may benefit from including the following information, subject to the official application requirements: Problem statement Clearly explain the educational or workforce challenge the proposed tool intends to address. Target users Identify the learners, educators, institutions, researchers or other groups that will use or benefit from the solution. Proposed solution Describe how the tool, platform, dataset or infrastructure will work. Evidence and rationale Explain the research, learning science, user feedback or practical evidence supporting the approach. Expected outcomes Describe how the proposed solution could improve learning, teaching, assessment, career navigation or education research. Implementation plan Explain how the solution will be developed, tested, introduced or used in real-world settings. Safety and privacy measures Describe how the proposal will address data protection, responsible AI, accessibility, fairness and user safety. Sustainability plan Explain how the tool or dataset can be maintained, improved and used over time. Applicants should rely on the official submission form and rules for the precise format, documentation and information required. Submit a proposal through the official competition website: Submit to the 2027 Tools Competition Competition Information Session The organisers have announced an information session for prospective applicants. Interested participants can register for the information session scheduled for: Date: September 15, 2026 The session may provide additional guidance about the competition, its tracks, eligibility, application process and expectations for proposals. Register for the 2027 Tools Competition information session Applicants should confirm the session time, format and registration requirements through the official registration page. Application Deadline The provided competition overview announces that the 2027 Tools Competition is live , but it does not state a final application deadline. Application Deadline: Not specified in the provided competition overview. Applicants should visit the official submission page, official rules and relevant track pages for the latest deadline information. Since competition timelines may be updated, prospective applicants should avoid relying on unofficial deadlines or outdated announcements. Organisers and Programme Partners The 2027 Tools Competition is supported and organised by two organisations: Renaissance Philanthropy Renaissance Philanthropy is identified as the programme behind the Tools Competition. The organisation supports initiatives intended to advance innovation and address important challenges through philanthropic investment and strategic programmes. Visit Renaissance Philanthropy The Learning Agency The Learning Agency is responsible for organising the Tools Competition. The organisation works on initiatives related to learning, education, research, innovation and the development of tools that can improve learning outcomes. Visit The Learning Agency How to Prepare a Strong Proposal Applicants can improve their readiness by taking the following steps: 1. Select the most appropriate track Review all four tracks and identify which one best matches the purpose of the proposed tool or dataset. Avoid submitting a general idea that does not clearly align with a competition priority. 2. Define the problem precisely Explain the problem in clear language. Identify who experiences the problem, why it matters and what limitations exist in current approaches. 3. Demonstrate user need Use research, interviews, surveys, pilot findings, classroom experience or other evidence to show that the problem is real and significant. 4. Explain what makes the solution different Describe how the proposed tool improves on existing approaches. The difference may involve better accessibility, stronger evidence, improved usability, greater inclusiveness, better data quality or more effective implementation. 5. Include evidence of feasibility Explain whether the team has already developed a prototype, conducted a pilot, tested the concept or gathered feedback from potential users. If the solution is still at an early stage, clearly describe the next steps. 6. Address responsible innovation Explain how the proposal will handle privacy, safety, fairness, accessibility, transparency and responsible use of artificial intelligence or data. 7. Plan for real-world adoption Consider how the tool will be used by schools, educators, learners, institutions, researchers or other stakeholders. A proposal should demonstrate awareness of practical constraints such as cost, training, infrastructure and user support. 8. Review the official rules Before submission, applicants should read the official rules, confirm eligibility and ensure that their proposal meets the required format and criteria. Conclusion The 2027 Tools Competition presents a major opportunity for innovators, researchers, education technology developers, organisations and data specialists working to improve learning, teaching and access to opportunity. Through its four tracks—Strengthening Teaching, Reimagining Assessment, Navigating Postsecondary Learning and Work, and Building Better Datasets—the competition seeks solutions that address real challenges across K–12 education, postsecondary learning, career transitions and education research. The competition’s focus extends beyond technological novelty. It encourages tools that are evidence-informed, practical, inclusive, safe, privacy-conscious and capable of producing meaningful outcomes in real learning environments. Potential applicants should carefully review the relevant track, complete the official eligibility check, read the competition rules and confirm the final submission deadline. The information provided in the competition overview does not specify a final deadline, so applicants should consult the official website for the latest updates.
